The film opens with the collision itself: one car carries a dead man on its windscreen and a screaming girl in the boot, and armed men step out of the vehicles. It then rewinds two days. Johan, head of security at a company run by a relative, is entangled in corrupt deals with the feared crime lord Bra Sol, and when one deal is jeopardized he counts on a promotion that instead goes to a black woman, a blow to his racist assumptions. At home his marriage to the socialite Diane is strained, and their rebellious daughter skips school to spend time with her boyfriend Cecil, a singer, and his money-hungry friend Thando. When Nicole is kidnapped by Bra Sol, Johan and Diane race against time to save her, and her fate comes to depend on Cecil and Thando. In a parallel story, Dinoko, a struggling shopkeeper who pays protection money to Bra Sol, loses a lease to the Nigerian immigrant Adze and rallies other locals into xenophobic attacks on foreign-owned businesses, unaware that his daughter Palesa has fallen in love with Adze. The riots knock out traffic lights, setting the stage for the crash that binds the stories together, while subplots touch on bribery, a corrupt mayor and the trafficking of young girls.

Collision premiered on Netflix on 16 June 2022, timed to South Africa's Youth Day. Reception was mixed. Naledi de Wee of The South African praised its exceptional acting, unexpected twists, Ofentse Mwase's cinematography and engagement with racism, xenophobia and human trafficking, comparing it favorably with Netflix's other South African productions. Vivian Nneka Nwajiaku of Afrocritik gave it 2.5 out of 5, likening its structure to Crash but finding the plot scattered, the thrills scarce, the political statements half-hearted and the performances middling apart from Dabula's menacing yet gentle Bra Sol. Other reviewers similarly found it competently shot but confusing and poorly paced.

Cheve was ranked only the 11th deepest known cave in the world, but in 1990 explorers who poured green dye into the stream flowing into its mouth found the coloured water emerging near the base of the mountain, about 1.6 miles below the highest known entrance. If people could follow the full course of the water, Cheve would surpass the record holder, Veryovkina in Georgia's Abkhazia region. Stone, who had been exploring the system since the late 1980s, led the 2021 expedition, the largest push yet, which drew 69 cavers from nine countries. The film presents the training, planning and safety precautions behind the descent, likened to climbing Everest in reverse, as the team rigs miles of rope down precipitous drops, wades underground rivers and moves between a chain of camps established ever deeper in the cave, sleeping underground for days or weeks at a time while searching for new passages that might lead further down. Over the expedition the cavers spent more than 1,500 cumulative nights underground and discovered more than 12 miles of unexplored passages, but by the end the team still did not know exactly how deep Cheve goes.

Alex Reif of Laughing Place wrote that, as with many such documentaries, the thrill of the special lay less in the destination than in the journey, and wrote that viewers would come away hoping National Geographic would document the team's next expedition. National Geographic magazine published an accompanying feature on the expedition by Maya Wei-Haas, with photographs by Kasia Biernacka.

The documentary begins before Toy Story, with Docter recalling Pixar's early years and how the studio moved from short films toward a planned Christmas special that eventually grew into the feature-length Toy Story. It then opens Pixar's archives to show early designs for Buzz, including the many alternative looks and names the character might have had, and explains how the team arrived at the toy that audiences came to know. The film examines Buzz's cultural impact and his meaning for Pixar's own artists. It then turns to MacLane, seen as a young member of the Toy Story 2 team; Docter describes him as the go-to authority on everything about Buzz, which helps explain why he was chosen to bring the character back in an origin story. The final section follows the making of Lightyear, detailing how the original action-figure design was translated into a believable human astronaut and the new challenges this created, while reflecting on what lies "beyond infinity."

The documentary premiered on Disney+ on 10 June 2022, a week before Lightyear opened in theaters on 17 June. Reviews were positive. Jacob Throneberry of Ready Steady Cut called it an exciting and insightful behind-the-scenes look, praising its brisk pace and the archival material on Buzz's origins, which he found more interesting than the account of Lightyear's production, and warned that it contains slight spoilers for the film. Jeremy Brown of What's On Disney Plus gave it four and a half stars, calling it his favorite of the studio's behind-the-scenes documentaries and saying it heightened his excitement for Lightyear.

In Green Hills, Sonic leads Tails and Knuckles off the path to the library, where Knuckles has sworn to Maddie Wachowski to return her library books on time, explaining that he is taking a shortcut. Imitating detectives in movies, Sonic narrates the adventure aloud, and the others join in. He has secretly brought them to the junkyard, where Wade Whipple has reported strange noises at night. There they find Unit, an abandoned Badnik drone built by Dr. Robotnik, which is upgrading itself with scrap parts and plans to conquer the world. Its laser blasts a hole through Maddie's books; Knuckles charges in, but Unit traps him in an old refrigerator and flings him onto a town billboard. Sonic's homing attacks knock the robot down, but a stray part sprays paint in his face, and Tails' bola is deflected onto Sonic's legs. Grounded by the airborne drone, Sonic asks Unit what it really wants for itself rather than what Robotnik programmed it to want. The robot shyly confesses a passion for poetry and begins reciting its verses until sunset, when Knuckles returns and smashes it apart. Tails recovers Unit's still-working core and is allowed to keep it as his responsibility, though Knuckles remains suspicious when Unit vows to make the world cower before its poetry. Sonic narrates the end of the adventure as the team heads off for chili dogs.

The title plays on the line "E.T. phone home", and the junkyard hides references to the first two films, including the baseball scoreboard Knuckles punched through in the sequel.

Emma and Scarlett are adoptive sisters and rebel vampires who feed only on the wicked; unhindered by sunlight but vulnerable to silver and stakes, Emma hitches rides on country roads to lure predatory men. As children the girls lost their adoptive parents when vampires attacked the family home, and they were taken in by the vampire Thorn, while their younger sister Kate was hidden by their mother and believed dead. In fact she was rescued and raised by the hunter Bullseye. The sisters, estranged after falling out over a man, are reunited when Scarlett tracks Emma down and, after a fight, tells her that Kate is alive. The three share a rare blood type, which their parents had been using to develop a vaccine against vampirism, and Kate has now completed it. Thorn, who ordered the attack on their parents, wants revenge and control of the vaccine and sends his followers after Kate, forcing the sisters to join forces to protect her. Emma becomes involved with Marcus, a bounty hunter with a past connection to Scarlett, who later turns against them, while Frank, an agent of Federal Vampire Control, crosses their path, and the conflict builds to a final battle with Thorn and his band of undead.

The film was released on video on demand and digital platforms on 7 June 2022 and was poorly received. Jim Morazzini of Nerdly gave it 2 out of 5, calling it a checklist of horror and revenge clichés whose fight scenes improved as it went on, with Greene's brief appearance a highlight, though he found it professionally filmed. Ade Smith of Movies & Mania likened it to a slick pilot for a television series and judged it entertaining but vapid, while the Taliesin Meets the Vampires blog rated it 4 out of 10, citing plot holes and weak action.

JP (Lendeborg), a cheerful young Latino, works a dead-end job at the local Lady Liberty's burger joint, while his sister Lily (Yumarie Morales) has won a place at Columbia University. During her celebration, agents of Immigration and Customs Enforcement raid the house. Governor Harper Finn (Cullen), seeking conservative votes for his re-election, has issued an executive order to arrest not only undocumented immigrants but also their children and JP and his sister are taken into detention. In the holding camp JP is offered a deal: if he volunteers to work as a carer at the Owl Cove retirement home, his charges will be dropped. He starts the job alongside the petty criminal Big Mac (Maldonado), the tough activist Camila (Ortega), the asthmatic conspiracy theorist Chris (Jorge Diaz) and Micah (Bella Ortiz), an Argentine who looks surprisingly white. The residents are strangely apathetic but prone to sudden fits of rage, and one elderly woman keeps trying to warn JP about something. When Chris vanishes after an escape attempt, leaving his inhaler behind, JP digs deeper. He discovers that residents and carers alike are being dosed with hormones that make their flesh tender, with the side effects of dementia and rapid ageing, so that the detainees can be ground into meat for the governor's burger chain; the old woman who tried to warn him is Lily. Micah turns out to be a plant spying on the carers. JP and his friends lead a revolt with the residents, the scheme is exposed, and Finn flees.

Magda is a headstrong careerist who has organized her whole life around her job and keeps every aspect of it under control, except for one weakness: a dislike of dachshunds rooted in a childhood trauma. On the very day she is due to be promoted, her boss asks her to look after her dachshund for the afternoon. Magda reluctantly agrees, but the dog falls ill, and her boss, blaming her, cancels the promotion and fires her. Hoping to win back her job by proving that she is in fact a dachshund lover, Magda learns of a dachshund parade held in Kraków and travels there to take part. In the city she rents a room from Krzysztof, a young widower who shares an apartment with his son Karol and their dachshund Trombone, without telling them that she has entered their lives for professional reasons. Despite her reservations, she gradually warms to the family, the dog included, and over the following days a connection grows between her and Krzysztof. As the parade approaches, Magda must choose between the career she has been fighting to restore and the promise of a new life.

Heart Parade was released on Netflix on 15 June 2022. Reviews were mixed to negative. Alex Wiggan of It's a Stampede! called it a bright, breezy and whimsical film with splashes of humor that simply sets out to entertain, praising Próchniak's authority and likeability, Rajski's ease as Karol and the attractive views of Kraków, while acknowledging its well-worn story and obvious outcome. Daniel Hart of Ready Steady Cut found it a meandering romantic comedy with little spark, crediting the lead actress's performance but criticizing the lack of chemistry between Magda and Krzysztof and the boredom of its third act.

A narrator recounts how, a century earlier, the mill town of Pleasant Bay, Oregon, fell on hard times when a drought closed its mill, until on Christmas Eve young Jimmy Stubbins found a strip of golden jingle bells that had fallen from Santa's sleigh and wished for the town's fortunes to be restored. By the next morning the river was flowing again and the mill was reopening. The bells became a symbol of hope, were put on display at the town museum and have been credited with Pleasant Bay's prosperity ever since. In the present, three days before Christmas, the bells are stolen, and the sheriff arrests George Bottoms, who works at the museum and has a past brush with the law, as the only person apparently able to reach them. Mayor Donovan, more concerned about his re-election than the town, is furious. Convinced that George is innocent, Violet, who has absorbed police procedure from watching her father and his bumbling deputy, the mayor's son, sets out with Kenny to find the real thief before Christmas, enlisting Maddie and Kenny's resentful brother Harrison. As the four uncover evidence the police overlooked, a romance grows between the teenagers, and their search leads into the underground tunnels beneath the town.

The film premiered on HBO Max on 24 November 2022. Liz Kocan of Decider recommended it as a sweet, Scooby-gang style whodunnit that turns into a Goonies-like adventure in its last third, praising McGraw's grounded performance, though she felt Bridges deserved a better role. Ricky Valero of Ready Steady Cut called it predictable but cute and enjoyed its score, while Barbara Shulgasser-Parker of Common Sense Media described it as a solid, kid-centred holiday movie.

The film opens with a montage of old illustrations of demons, skydivers performing a risky manoeuvre and blood being dripped onto an altimeter as it is assembled, ending with one of the parachutists falling to their death. Ten years later, Sarah (Adams), an avid skydiver like her late father, is the new member of a local skydiving club. Payson (Holcomb) is eager for her to join his team of Lisa (Berman), Wade (Roberts), Evan (Alperin) and Greg (Worch), because he wants to attempt The Hex, the dangerous and allegedly cursed formation jump that went wrong a decade earlier; the only ominous presence at the drop zone is Kris (Mozingo), a grizzled old parachute packer. The team pulls off the formation, but one of them never lands, vanishing in mid-air and even disappearing from the video of the jump. When the group jumps again the next day, another member suffers a heart attack on the way down, and further deaths follow, from a body found with every bone broken to an exploding apartment. Sarah, who seems to be the only one unaware that her father died performing The Hex along with the rest of his team, is drawn into a story of curses and deals with demons.

Reviews were negative. Jim Morazzini of Voices From the Balcony, in a review republished by Nerdly, gave it two out of five, calling it a waste of potential, "Point Break reaches its Final Destination"; he admired some impressive jump footage and the initially intriguing mystery, but found the script full of obvious twists and gaping plot holes, the deaths random and the gore light. Brian Costello of Common Sense Media described an interesting premise lost in flawed execution and clunky storytelling, with low-budget limitations increasingly evident, though he found its depiction of skydiving culture partly believable.

After their coronation as king and queen of Liones, Meliodas, of the Demon Clan, and Elizabeth, of the Goddess Clan, have a son, Tristan, who inherits the powers of both parents. At ten, while training with Lancelot, the son of Ban and a fairy, Tristan loses control to the demon side of his nature and gravely injures his friend, who vanishes shortly after. Ashamed and frightened of losing control again, Tristan turns to the gentler, healing side of his abilities, straining his bond with his parents.

Four years later Elizabeth falls gravely ill from a curse cast by Priest, a servant of Deathpierce, a former Holy Knight who seeks revenge for the injustices he suffered at the hands of the Demon and Goddess Clans fourteen years earlier. Tristan's goddess powers cannot cure his mother, so when he senses Priest he rushes out of the kingdom alone to save her. Gowther tracks him and alerts their old companions from the disbanded Seven Deadly Sins. Meanwhile Deathpierce is capturing demons, giants and fairies and fusing them into monstrous chimeras with his mystical Chaos Staff, planning to use them to conquer Liones.

On the road Tristan meets a hostile fairy who has rescued three non-human children from the Empties, the magical automatons serving Deathpierce. Uneasy allies, the pair trail the captive parents of those children to Edinburgh, the stronghold Deathpierce rules, and free them. When Tristan is nearly killed while struggling to master his demonic instincts, the fairy saves him and takes on a human form, revealing himself to be Lancelot.

Netflix released the film on December 20, 2022, with Part 2 following in August 2023. Anime News Network gave it a B-minus, enjoying the chance to reconnect with the characters and their children and calling it the start of a pretty good adventure, while IGN found it entertaining but incomplete.

At a junkyard where the face-tattooed henchmen of the psychotic drug lord Temple (Jones) are about to execute a man who betrayed them, a skilled thief known only as the Thief (Clayton) sneaks in, grabs a large stash of cash, fights off the gang amid a hail of bullets and escapes in a stolen car. After a collision forces him to take another vehicle, he pulls over on the highway to bandage a wound and discovers a stowaway hiding in the trunk: Mia (Lecompte), Temple's pregnant wife, who has fled because she refuses to raise her child with such a brutal father, and who overheard the Thief's getaway plan. Furious at both the robbery and her betrayal, Temple sends his associate Skinny (Mac) and his top enforcer, a seemingly unstoppable assassin known as the Frenchman (Katabarwa), to recover the money, Mia and his unborn child. The reluctant partners go on the run with Temple's killers on their trail, their escape complicated by a stop at a clinic for Mia's pregnancy and by a gang of local thugs who try to steal the money for themselves.

Reviews were mixed to negative. Julian Roman of MovieWeb praised the strong, Guy Ritchie-style opening, the groovy soundtrack, the chemistry between Clayton and Lecompte and Jones and Katabarwa as sadistic villains, but felt a filler-heavy second act brought the film to a crawl, recommending it only as a pure B-movie. AMovieGuy.com gave it two stars out of four, crediting Clayton's energy and quick editing but finding the action mundane, the leads' chemistry ice cold and Jones underused. Ewan Gleadow of Cult Following criticised its generic storytelling, poorly developed action and blurred, trailer-like visuals.

Lena is a teenager whose parents have uprooted their lives and found new jobs so that the family can move to Oslo and give her a fresh start after a scandal in her previous town, the reasons for which are not revealed at first. At her new school, which the royal twins attend, she strikes up a friendly conversation with Kalle on her first day. The prince, who is trying to shake off his party-boy image and is weary of people who see only his public persona, takes a liking to her, and the two slowly begin a romance through a series of ups and downs, including surprise visits to her home and the pressures of life in the public eye. Lena, who seems unimpressed that she is dating a royal, is not completely honest with Kalle about why she moved, and the secret she carries keeps haunting her; she devotedly cares for a baby she introduces to classmates as her little brother, though the child's real connection to her is more complicated. Her past catches up with her through old friends she treated badly, while the protective Margrethe, determined to preserve the royal status quo, makes biting remarks about Lena's ordinary background and opposes the relationship. As the truth threatens to come out, Lena must decide what she is willing to reveal to keep her love.

Royalteen was released on Netflix on 17 August 2022. Reviews were mixed. Decider's Radhika Menon advised skipping it, finding the romance clunky, Lena's secret obvious from the first act and the ending confusing, though she praised the strong chemistry between Asserson and Storhøi and the parents' grounded performances. On High on Films, Akash Deshpande considered the premise a reiteration of familiar teen tropes with surface-level class commentary, but found it consistently engaging thanks to unhurried direction and committed acting. Norwegian newspaper VG was more enthusiastic.

The film notes that scientific study of cats lags roughly fifteen years behind research on dogs, and that holding cats to canine expectations has long been a mistake: cats show affection and loyalty but are not driven to please their owners. Combining interviews, archival footage, animated sequences and viral cat videos, it examines the animals' unusual skeletal structure and balance, the many vocalisations they use, including meows directed at humans to win a response, and signs of trust such as slow blinking or lying belly up. It asks whether cats know their own names, play favourites and truly love their owners. A historical thread traces how cats largely domesticated themselves by hunting rodents for early farmers, cites ancient remains found in Cyprus as evidence of the long human bond, describes how the persecution of cats in medieval Europe may have helped plague spread, and features Herman, a cat enlisted with the US Coast Guard in the 1940s, as well as Istanbul's protective approach to street cats. The Savitsky Cats demonstrate that felines can be trained through techniques such as clicker training and positive reinforcement.

The documentary was released on Netflix on 18 August 2022. Joel Keller of Decider recommended it as a family-friendly starting point for new and prospective cat owners, enjoying its adorable subjects and the acrobatic Savitsky Cats while noting that much of its information is available elsewhere and that it does not go deeply into topics such as indoor versus outdoor living. Greg Wheeler of The Review Geek rated it 7.5 out of 10, calling it fun and informative though rushed in its final minutes, and Common Sense Media described it as a purr-fect primer for children.

Kim (Fish) is a workaholic who keeps working even during her office Christmas party and ignores her colleague's and her mother's urging to take time off. While hailing a taxi one night she clashes with Mark (James), another busy professional, and makes him late for an important meeting; as a result his boss, who favours his own inexperienced son, fires Mark. When Kim's boyfriend Steven (Purvis) breaks up with her instead of proposing because she is always busy, her mother Mary (Whyte) whisks her away to a week-long Christmas retreat in the mountains to reconnect with the spirit of the holiday. There they meet the retreat's owner Rae (Fawcett) and her newly unemployed brother Mark, who has come to clear his head, while Mary reunites with her friend Celeste (Lynn) and Celeste's older brother Ted (MacDonald), a retired photographer. The retreat's first rule bans all electronic devices, but Kim hides her phone in a sock to keep up with work and with Steven; when Mark catches her, she points out that he has kept his too, and they agree not to report each other. Through gingerbread house and wreath making, Christmas storytelling and a visit to a pancake restaurant, Kim and Mark overcome their mutual hostility and the mistakes neither wants to admit, and slowly fall for each other, while a romance also blossoms between Mary and Ted.

Reviews were mixed. Markos Papadatos of True Hollywood Talk gave the film four out of five stars, calling it a heartwarming, feel-good film that held the viewer's attention, with good chemistry between the charming James and the bubbly, sassy Fish, and describing Whyte as sensational as Mary. Nick Wangersky of the Canadian film site HNMag found it predictable from start to finish, with leads who were not especially likeable and supporting characters who were not around long enough, though he enjoyed the mountain setting.

Emma is a senior vice president at a successful toy company in Chicago who feels she lives Christmas all year round. She once loved the holiday, but spending twelve months a year thinking about it has left her no time for dating or much else, and after a strong year in which she developed one of the season's most successful toys, a K-pop panda, she is exhausted. All she wants is a holiday-free getaway at a tropical singles resort, so she asks her assistant and friend Lucy to book her a trip to St. John in the Caribbean. Because of a booking mix-up, however, she lands in St. John, Alaska, dressed in sandals and a strapless jumpsuit, in sub-zero temperatures, in a small town devoted to everything Christmas. When a snowstorm shuts the airport, she is stranded. Connor, a local holiday hero who considers her a Scrooge, gives her his coat and a ride to the Sleigh Bell Inn, run by his sister Callie and her wife, where Emma is checked into the festive Candy Cane Suite. As Connor shows her the town, from snowball fights and snowshoeing to the toys he makes for local children, Emma's childhood memories of Christmas begin to thaw her, until she discovers that Connor has a connection to her work that he has kept from her, and the two must sort out their feelings before she flies home.

Reviews were mostly negative. Kristen of TV Tweetie found the premise cute, comparing Emma's predicament to Home Alone 2, and liked Wilson and Ruttle in the leads, especially the caring Connor, but she judged the film flawed by a slow start, clichés and errors such as characters standing outdoors without hats or gloves in temperatures said to be twelve below zero, and did not recommend it. Patrick Serrano of Lifetime Uncorked gave it his lowest ratings, describing its plot as erratic and the result as almost a parody of a bad TV movie, though he welcomed its depiction of a lesbian couple.

The film's participants include the physicists Brian Greene, Janna Levin, Stephon Alexander, Carlo Rovelli and Anthony Aguirre, the astrophysicist Delilah Gates, the mathematicians Steven Strogatz, Eugenia Cheng and Moon Duchin, the philosophers Rebecca Goldstein and Kenny Easwaran, and the physicist and novelist Alan Lightman. Organised into numbered chapters and illustrated by animation in a wide range of styles, from the literal to the metaphorical, it asks whether infinity exists, whether it can be found in the physical world, and whether a mortal person could ever experience the endless. Strogatz narrates "The Infinite Hotel", a cartoon based on the German mathematician David Hilbert's thought experiment about a fully occupied hotel that can always find room for more guests, even infinitely many. Other segments consider how infinity can make one equal zero, the very large and the very small, black holes and wormholes, and an apple left in a box for so long that it decays into particles and eventually becomes an apple again. Gates reflects on whether the universe might be finite yet appear endless to its inhabitants, like a dot travelling round a circle or across the surface of a ball, and the film notes that there are infinitely many ways for the universe to be finite but only a few for it to be infinite. The film closes by asking whether human creativity itself is infinite, leaving the impression that infinity reveals the limits of human understanding.

A Trip to Infinity won the award for Outstanding Graphic Design and Art Direction at the 44th News and Documentary Emmy Awards. John Serba of Decider found it slickly made and terrifically entertaining without dumbing down its ideas, singling out Strogatz's infectious enthusiasm. In The New Yorker, the mathematician Dan Rockmore praised its experts and the Infinite Hotel sequence but felt that its psychedelic animations and philosophical detours sometimes distracted from the mathematics.

On the day before her thirtieth birthday, Sofia, a graphic designer, is fired from her job by her eccentric boss, then comes home to catch her live-in boyfriend of many years, Richard, cheating on her, and breaks her foot falling down the stairs as she storms out. She moves back in with her widowed mother Lainie for the summer to start again from scratch. Worried that her cynical daughter will slip back into a job she hates and a relationship that is wrong for her, Lainie signs the two of them up for a couples' cooking class, where Sofia meets Matias, a charming aspiring chef visiting from Spain, who is helping his uncle Guillermo teach. When Lainie conveniently drops out, Sofia and Matias are paired together and soon become friends. With the encouragement of Lainie, Matias and her high school friend Olivia, Sofia begins to rebuild her professional and social life and considers going back to school for a master's degree. Her blossoming romance is complicated when Richard tries to win her back and when she learns that Matias has a girlfriend, whom Sofia refuses to wrong as she was wronged. Along the way the group celebrates the Spanish tradition of Saint John's Eve, Sofia learns that her mother once loved another man before marrying her father and sets out to reunite them, and the story culminates in an airport chase as Sofia decides what she wants.

The film was released on Netflix on 25 August 2022. Reviews described it as pleasant but formulaic. Jonathon Wilson of Ready Steady Cut called it innocuous, enjoyable comfort food that clung too rigidly to romcom clichés and lacked real conflict. Alia Shirazi of The Envoy praised Dandy, Lenehan and Tur but found little chemistry between the leads, while Emily Tsiao of Plugged In found the story sweet but criticised its language and sexual content for family viewers.

Harper McNevin (Davis), a Christmas enthusiast who cares deeply about the meaning of gifts, runs and promotes a Six Degrees of Santa programme with her daughter Dani. Each year they hand out special boxes: one person places a gift in a box and passes it anonymously to a second person, who enjoys it briefly before re-gifting it to a third, and so on until six degrees of separation lie between the original giver and the final recipient, who keeps it. Harper secretly puts a copy of her favourite book, Northbound Elf, in a box with a personal note and gives it to her mail carrier, who reads it to his son before passing it on. The book eventually reaches Jason Sparks (Lund), a workaholic internet entrepreneur whose Sparkle Trees venture aims to make Christmas tree delivery easier, an idea he had when his sick uncle could not get a tree. Northbound Elf was Jason's own childhood favourite and he had lost his copy, so he takes the gift and its note as a sign of fate and becomes convinced that the first Santa in the chain might be his soulmate. He tracks down Harper, as the programme's creator, to help him find her. Not wanting Jason to know that she sent the book, Harper persuades her neighbour to pose as the first Santa and go on dates with him, while she and Jason, who initially got off on the wrong foot, get to know each other and gradually fall in love.

Gissane Sophia of Lady Geeks Media found the film fun even when it was laughable, praising its premise as a delightful twist on White Elephant and Secret Santa exchanges and its romance as natural, pleasantly surprising and built on partnership, and noting that the eventual revelation of Harper's secret avoids a blowout argument. Kristen of TV Tweetie liked the cute concept but felt the film moved at a snail's pace, especially in its first half, and lacked the music, memorable scenes and spark needed for a really good Christmas movie.

Lan-hsin (Lu), nearing retirement, has run a children's art studio and day care for more than thirty years. Her income has helped put her children through college and pay for a family apartment, where she once also cared for her father-in-law in his final years, and her own artistic ambitions have shrunk to painting the tiny items in the studio's dolls' house. At home, her retired husband David (Kou), a hoarder of supposedly valuable teapots and broken appliances, will not lift a finger, issues constant instructions and throws out her books to make room. Her cold, critical mother (Paw), who discouraged her dreams, including studying in Paris, is slipping into dementia and keeps wandering out of her nursing home. Her architect daughter (Chia) quietly confides that she has quit her job, broken up with her boyfriend and is moving back home, while her son, a college teacher in the United States, is considering returning with his wife to take over her family's farm, and her sister-in-law presses her with a get-rich-quick scheme selling upmarket cemetery plots. Believing that a bigger place will make her family happy, Lan-hsin sets out to find a new house large enough for all of them and weighs investment opportunities, at one point appearing to be defrauded by a young estate agent she knows, as the film, framed by her complaints to her mother, raises questions about whether some events are real or imagined and whether she will reclaim something for herself.

Reviews were mixed. Roger Moore of Movie Nation saw it as a kind of upside-down The Joy Luck Club steeped in Stella Dallas-style martyrdom, with interesting subtexts about Taiwanese family duty and gambling culture, but felt that Wang let scenes linger so long that 95 minutes of material played out over 124, muddling the message. Brian Hioe of Cinema Escapist found the focus on a woman on the verge of retirement promising but judged that the film lacked dramatic punch and focus, introducing the fraud subplot and doubts about the narrator's reliability too late to succeed.

Teez, a former Detroit Lions player whose first NFL paycheque in 2017 was eroded by agent fees, taxes, two houses and holidays, is anxious about making the most of what remains as injury stalls his career; McDonald urges him to put money into a stock index fund while he tries out for the Chicago Bears. Kim and John, a couple from Boulder, Colorado, whose life-coaching business thrived on video calls during lockdown, are told by Adeney that their large monthly expenses stand in the way of early retirement, raising the question of how frugal they want to be. Ariana, a married mother of two in New Jersey, is weighed down by credit card and student loan debt dating back to her post-graduate spending, and Aliche divides her salary into strict budget accounts. Lindsey, a bartender and waitress in Austin, Texas, works two jobs yet cannot pay her bills or afford treatment for her mental health, and Pant helps her replace one of them with side hustles drawing on her talent for art and fashion. Along the way the film cites statistics on financial insecurity, noting that Black families own less than two per cent of US stocks, and argues that most Americans are never taught how to manage money.

The documentary was released on Netflix on 6 September 2022. Jack Seale of The Guardian found its advice extremely basic and its case studies mostly comfortable, arguing that the film largely ignored people with no money to manage, though he considered Lindsey's story genuinely engaging. Sabrina McFarland of Common Sense Media praised it as a frank, timely look at financial literacy built around families from diverse economic backgrounds.

Joy (Sears) is a hard-working but uninspired sous chef at a big-city restaurant in New York, where she feels undervalued while striving for promotion to executive chef. Her boyfriend Gabe (Royce) has arranged, without consulting her, a Christmas visit to meet his family at their Vermont mansion. Because Gabe's mother is campaigning for mayor and needs his help, Joy must drive there alone in his expensive car, and while helping him pack she accidentally discovers an engagement ring in his luggage, leaving her uneasy about their future together. Meanwhile James Lewis (McLaren) is struggling to save his family's maple syrup farm, a legacy begun by his great-great-grandfather and maintained by his father, whose leftover debts are taking a toll; his brother David (Tobin) wants to sell. Heading to Vermont through a snowstorm, Joy skids on ice into a snowbank, and Gabe, busy with a press conference for his mother, simply tells her to call a tow truck. James, out on an errand, finds her and takes her to the farm to stay while her car is repaired. Joy, whom James nicknames JJ, loves the peaceful countryside and the warm, welcoming Lewis family, and when young Riley (Cannon) begs her to help save the farm, she comes up with a plan that gets the whole family involved. Rethinking her priorities, Joy realises what has been missing in her life as sparks fly between her and James.

Reception was divided. The family-oriented Dove review, contributed by Super Channel, called it a beautiful Christmas film approved for all ages and praised its message about close-knit families and following one's heart. Wholesome Romance Movies gave it perfect scores, singling out the cabin setting and the inviting family. Cassandra Morgan, however, advised against watching it, finding it slow and boring and complaining that its love triangle failed because Gabe was so dreadful, repeatedly putting his mother's wishes before Joy's needs, that neither suitor seemed a viable option.

Ivy brings a new book about ballet to her best friend Bean's house. Its grand tales of queens and sword fights fire the girls' imaginations, prompting a fantasy sequence, and they decide to sign up for ballet lessons. Ivy's mother (Dotin) agrees readily, but Bean's mother (House) is sceptical, since Bean has already quit trumpet lessons, softball and gymnastics, and Bean's snarky older sister Nancy (Jewett) bets her ten dollars that she will not finish the course. Arriving at class in capes and carrying weapons, expecting sword fighting, the girls quickly discover that there will be no kicking or dancing to the death. Their pretentious instructor, Monsieur Joie (Ferguson), who peppers his speech with exaggerated French, is unimpressed and sidelines the two awkward dancers by casting them as friendly squid in a big upcoming recital in front of hundreds of people. Desperate to escape, Ivy dons her cape and tries a forgetting spell on their mothers, made with gross ingredients including dead flies, but it fails. Ivy's mother says she may quit, believing children must try things to learn who they are, while Bean's mother insists that Bean finish what she started for once. In a show of loyalty, Ivy agrees to stick it out alongside her friend, and the pair hatch a series of schemes to get out of the performance as the recital approaches.

Reviews were generally favourable. John Serba of Decider recommended it as easily the best of the three films, praising its subversion of the series' formula, the reduced gross-out humour and the sense that the girls' friendship deepens with each mishap, and enjoyed Ferguson's doltish instructor. Common Sense Media judged it the weakest of the trilogy but still good, sweet fun, highlighting Ferguson's campy turn and the delightful central friendship.

Having become best friends in the first film, the two imaginative girls now do their best to stay inseparable at school. Slipping in through a back door to the teachers' restroom, Ivy notices old pipes rattling near the ceiling and wisps drifting from the vents and concludes that the school, supposedly built on top of graves, is haunted, picturing ghosts in a skull-filled underworld cemetery beneath it. Since the girls' fantasies are often shown on screen, it remains doubtful that the ghosts are real, but Ivy, who keeps a dead frog in a bag in the fridge, consults a creepy spell book and plans a potion to send the spirits away. Dressing in a cape and dark makeup, she rounds up classmates to help, while the pair keep landing on the timeout rug and try to avoid Mrs. Noble, a shoe-loving, dragon-like figure whom the students suspect of locking children in a closet. One ingredient of the spell is a lock of Nancy's hair, cut after midnight, which leads to a nighttime raid on her bedroom amid Nancy's own campaign to get her ears pierced. The plan requires sneaking into the school at night, and the climax ends with the girls accidentally flooding the school bathroom. They are duly punished, but before being sent to their rooms they swear a sweet oath of friendship.

The film premiered on Netflix on 2 September 2022. Common Sense Media's Jennifer Green rated it suitable for ages six and up, calling it good, innocent fun that captures childhood energy and ingenuity, praising Lynch's gusto and its messages about friendship and the responsible use of imagination, while noting potentially scary ghost imagery and pee and fart jokes. John Serba of Decider recommended it, judging Lynch's mean principal an improvement on the first film's villain and praising the series for celebrating friendship, imagination and mischief, though he found some classmates dull and the toilet-flooding climax overly noisy.

The film recounts the controversial transfer in the summer of 2000 of the Portuguese footballer Figo from Barcelona to their bitter rivals Real Madrid, in the same year he won the Ballon d'Or. Opening with a brooding Figo behind the wheel of a car, insisting that while many people think they know the story, only he knows the truth, it combines archive footage with the testimony of those involved. To explain why the move was seen as such a betrayal, it sets out the cultural and political divide between Catalonia and Madrid, including the legacy of Franco's dictatorship, with Guardiola, Figo's former roommate and confidant, describing what Barcelona means to Catalans. It follows Pérez's campaign for the Real Madrid presidency, in which he promised to sign Figo if elected and to pay the membership fees of every member if he failed, his use of the sports press, and his media sparring with Gaspart. The negotiations led by Veiga and Pérez's associates build to a deal that, despite Figo repeatedly saying he wanted to stay at Barcelona, made the seemingly impossible inevitable. The world-record fee of around £37 million launched Real Madrid's Galácticos era and, the film argues, reshaped the transfer market. The directors said they deliberately structured it as a heist movie focused on a three-week period.

Liam Miller of Urban Pitch praised its gripping mix of jaw-dropping archive footage and candid interviews, saying it shattered simplistic good-versus-evil accounts of the saga and showed that the player is the least important part of a transfer. RobScene rated it 6/10, calling it an accomplished, engrossing and compelling account in which the participants contradict one another, but felt it was too long and lingered too much on the negotiations at the expense of the aftermath.

The documentary follows the roughly three-year effort to bring the series from concept to screen, leading up to its launch around Star Wars Celebration in May 2022. It opens with period interview footage of Alec Guinness, the original Obi-Wan, in costume describing the challenge of playing the role, and later shows McGregor watching Guinness on a big screen. Drawing on never-before-seen behind-the-scenes footage, it presents the return of Obi-Wan Kenobi and Anakin Skywalker and of McGregor and Christensen to their roles, centring on the reunion of the two actors, who had last appeared together in Revenge of the Sith in 2005, with archival footage of George Lucas at work as director and of Carrie Fisher as Princess Leia. Chow discusses the responsibility of continuing a legacy character and defends making the young Leia, played by Blair, central to the story, while Blair recalls discovering Star Wars through books. The film also visits the creature shop and props department and shows the show's lightsabers, costumes and sets.

Reviewers largely saw it as a piece for devoted fans. Liberty Lester of CultureSlate felt it favoured an emotional, cinematic portrait over a nuts-and-bolts account and conveyed the evident love of everyone involved, especially McGregor's boyish enthusiasm. Miguel Fernandez of Star Wars News Net found it a longer, more detailed version of the series' promotional featurettes that could have gone deeper into the creative process. The Times of India called it a must-watch for hardcore Star Wars fans, redeemed mainly by its archival footage, but questioned the decision to release it after the series rather than before.

Sunny is investigating the murders of two women whose bodies were dismembered to remove their sweat glands. At the same time she is consumed by her affair with the married Juro and desperate to keep her sensual hold on him, a struggle made harder by her inability to smell. In the course of the investigation she encounters Dorian, a suspect who is trying to distill the essence of love even if it means drawing on gruesome sources, and she suspects that he may hold the key to restoring her lost sense. When she discovers that one of his compounds has an irresistible effect on Juro, she cannot resist using it. The detective and the suspected killer enter an uneasy partnership in which Dorian tries to help Sunny regain her sense of smell through both physical and psychological methods, seeking to unlock something buried inside her. Dorian, who admits he has never known love, wonders whether he can still create it, and the film explores the links between scent, desire and obsession through surreal, neon-lit imagery, with Sunny narrating the story in voice-over throughout.

Austin Craig (Frey), a quick-witted brand strategist, works with his childhood friend Tipper Tisdale (Walder), and the pair are close to landing an event that could take their business to the next level when each receives a mysterious letter from Mrs. Marley, a beloved old neighbour who has recently died. Growing up, Mrs. Marley and her husband opened their large house to the neighbourhood children, hosting an annual Candy Cane Carnival and a Christmas treasure hunt every year, and in her letter she invites the six childhood friends to reunite in their hometown of Belleville for one last hunt. Her death has hit Everett Matthews (Massey), Austin's former best friend, especially hard, since he cared for her in her final years. While he is decorating her old house for Christmas on his own, their friend Ricky Treviño (Aguire) brings the bad news that the house will be sold to a land developer and turned into a ski resort unless Everett can raise $200,000. Everett is determined to find Mrs. Marley's buried treasure to save it, while Austin hopes to use part of the money to build his company. As the friends, including Michelle Wu (McKenzie) and the professional basketball player Clay King (Towns), follow her clues and contend with a scheming estate agent, Rochelle Raimo (Federici), Austin and Everett revisit their complicated history, including Everett's painful coming out, and the old sparks between them reignite.

Decider recommended the film, calling it "a lot of movie", with a larger lead cast and bigger premise than most holiday television films, but praising the multi-faceted, lived-in characterisations of the principal characters, Frey's snarky yet cuddly Austin, and a memorable fast-talking bluffing scene for Walder. The reviewer found the elaborate Marley backstory distracting and felt that two of the friends were underused, but concluded that the film understood that the most important parts were its small, intimate details.

The title refers to the moment, 1:14 p.m. on 19 September 2017, when an earthquake devastated Mexico City and its surroundings. As citizens mobilised to help, Zurita quickly organised a group of friends, including singers, actors, content creators and other celebrities, to raise money for reconstruction through the Love Army México initiative, and the project set out to build fifty homes for families affected by the quake in Ocuilan, in the State of Mexico. Through interviews, phone calls, video meetings and footage from the site, the film follows the troubled process that followed over the next four years: disagreements among the organisers, the discovery that construction costs exceeded commercial prices, money running out, and Zurita having to contribute his own funds, until 47 houses were finally delivered and the original goal was acknowledged as unmet. It also responds to accusations in the press that the donations had been mishandled, with media figures and friends of Zurita speaking in his defence.

The documentary premiered on Prime Video in September 2022 and drew a largely negative critical response in Mexico. Alejandro Badillo of Neotraba described it as an example of the white saviour complex, arguing that it used the people of Ocuilan as a backdrop to clear Zurita's name. Ernesto Eslava of Por si alguien preguntaba called it manipulative, noting that the affected residents speak for only a few minutes and that it never explains how the money was spent or the beneficiaries chosen, and the film critic Kristoff Raczynski, as reported by Milenio, dismissed it as one of the worst documentaries he had seen.

After the COVID-19 pandemic forced the cancellation of their Map of the Soul Tour, BTS, the top-grossing touring act of 2019, had spent nearly two years performing only to online audiences. The Los Angeles concerts were the band's first performances in front of an in-person crowd since 2019, and the film captures the reunion between the group and its fans, known as ARMY. Running about two and a half hours, the show opens with the members emerging from a cage for a marching-band version of "On", followed by "Fire", "Dope" and "DNA". Slower songs such as "Blue and Grey" and "Black Swan", performed with dancers in white-feathered sleeves, lead into a medley of "Blood Sweat & Tears" and "Fake Love" on a set inspired by their music videos, complete with waterfalls and giant sculpted hands. The band sings "Life Goes On" on a giant bed and then an oversized sofa, plays live-band versions of "Boy with Luv", "Dynamite" and "Butter", and performs B-sides including "Airplane pt. 2", "Silver Spoon", "Telepathy" and "So What", before an encore that builds to "Permission to Dance". Individual nights featured special guests, with Megan Thee Stallion joining a remix of "Butter" and Coldplay's Chris Martin performing "My Universe" with the group.

Holly (Lowndes) moved to New York five years earlier to pursue a career on Broadway. She has made it into the chorus a couple of times but has never landed a leading role, since casting directors love her voice but always find her too young, too old, too tall or too short. By day she works in a retail shop, where she sings as she works and some customers admit they come in just to hear her. One morning on her way to work she literally bumps into Jason (Greene), a father who writes jingles for local commercials and hopes to move up to national advertising campaigns. Holly's voice catches the attention of Cora (Knight), a property entrepreneur who owns the building that houses the shop and who wants to revive a community Christmas show that was a local tradition for decades. Convinced that Holly is the perfect voice to showcase, Cora pairs her with Jason to debut a new Christmas song he has written. As the two refine the song and their performance, and Holly bakes cookies with Jason's daughter Angela (Sellers), whose custody he shares, they discover they have more in common than music. Both are reluctant to get involved, however: Holly plans to leave New York if she has not landed a role by the end of the year, and Jason worries that Angela is growing attached to her, while Cora's encouragement offers Holly unexpected mentorship toward her dream career.

Reviews were mixed. Kristen of TV Tweetie found it enjoyable, cute and solid, praising Lowndes's amazing voice, Greene's performance and the special pleasure of hearing Knight perform, though she felt some of the heroine's decisions were out of character. Cassandra Morgan called the singing gorgeous and Knight a joy but considered the script weak and the plot boring, citing the underused Angela, who keeps leaving scenes, and a running joke about Holly's scarf that is quickly dropped.

In the small town of Icicle Falls, one street, Candy Cane Lane, is famous for going all out at Christmas, and its residents are expected to decorate their houses lavishly and welcome crowds of visitors. Ivy Donaldson (Barber) has found the season hard since the death a few years earlier of her mother, Muriel, the town's beloved queen of Christmas, who owned a Christmas shop and headed the committee that ran the street's festivities. Feeling it was her duty to carry on, Ivy took over the shop and moved into her mother's house to keep the Candy Cane Lane traditions alive, but she cannot escape constant comparisons with her mother. The pressure of living up to Muriel's standards has strained everything in her life: she is now separated from her husband Rob (Payne), and their teenage daughter Jordan (Cooper) is tired of their lives revolving around the neighbourhood's activities. As the holidays approach, someone starts tampering with the candy cane decorations across the street, and a series of strange but comic mishaps, including Ivy and Rob dressing up as Mr. and Mrs. Claus, brings the family back together in unexpected and festive ways, as Ivy learns to follow her own dreams rather than carry a legacy that has become a burden.

Reviews were unenthusiastic. Kristen of TV Tweetie found it cute but "kind of meh", praising the striking Claus costumes, the performances of Payne and Cooper as a husband and daughter hoping to reunite the family, and its message about letting go of traditions that are burdens rather than gifts, though she felt Barber's acting style was very familiar. Cassandra Morgan advised against watching it, arguing that it had a good premise but tried to be a comedy, a romance and a mystery at once without letting its slapstick jokes land.

Moving between several timelines, the film opens on a farm in the Turkish countryside decades earlier, where Bekir rules his family with an iron fist. His wife Havva resents his infidelity and the harshness with which he treats their children: he regularly slaps his eldest son Kadir, keeps the children out of school and records them with a video camera, while Saliha secretly meets Cemil, a boy with a remarkable singing voice who works on the farm, and young Yusuf is his father's favourite. After a particularly cruel punishment of Kadir, Bekir falls ill, and following the family's loss they move to the city. Some thirty years later Kadir, now a filmmaker, returns to the old house to shoot a film drawn from his childhood memories, recreating episodes such as the day his father punished him with a hosepipe. When the production stalls he stays on, and during the COVID-19 pandemic the family is reunited under the same roof: Havva, now suffering from dementia, has been released from her care home into Saliha's care, Saliha is divorced with a teenage daughter, and Yusuf, married with a son, is unhappy and frustrated that the farm has not been sold. As Kadir excavates their past, old tensions revive, Cemil and Saliha confront their unspoken romance, and painful family secrets come to light.

The film was released on Netflix on 27 October 2022. Marshall Shaffer of Decider recommended it as a modest meta-movie in the tradition of 8½, praising its exploration of the borders between reality and fiction and singling out Sürer's performance, while finding it overlong. Akash Deshpande of High on Films admired Yavru's photography and sound but found its shifts into comedy jarring, and Lori Meek of Ready Steady Cut praised the performances but called it a slow melodrama whose relationships remained underexplored.

Elle, a former class valedictorian who has become a powerhouse in the tech industry, is the class president of a group of high school classmates who once dubbed themselves the "cursed class" after a run of disasters stretching back to their senior winter formal and continuing through their previous reunions. Determined to break the bad luck, she meticulously plans their fifteen-year reunion at Christmas, only to find that much of it depends on Devin, the former class clown and vice-president, whose events company is supplying the equipment and who had not intended to attend. When fire and water damage leaves them scrambling for a new venue, the two opposites work together to find another location, and Elle comes to appreciate the spontaneous approach to life of Devin, a single father devoted to his teenage daughter and his business. At the same time her career unravels when the CEO of her company, whom she cannot reach, is reported to be under FBI investigation. Elle had also hoped to reconnect with her high school crush, Kam, but spending time with him shows her that what she wanted at seventeen is not what she needs now. Alongside them, classmates including Sam, a successful broadcaster who still feels invisible, and a pair of high school sweethearts going through a rough patch challenge one another to remember who they were, who they are and who they want to be.

The film premiered on Hallmark Channel on 10 December 2022 as part of its Countdown to Christmas season. Alonso Duralde of TheWrap ranked it 33rd of the network's 43 new holiday films of 2022, crediting a valiant attempt at a different kind of storytelling and an appealing cast but finding it undermined by contrivances and illogical character choices. Kristen of TV Tweetie called it predictable and ho-hum, though she liked Novlan.

Four years after her husband Brian (Edwards) died in a car accident, Kaitlyn (Williams) is raising their ten-year-old son Adam (Droulis) alone in Los Angeles, having moved away from Colorado because she could not bear to stay without him. Adam has grown increasingly withdrawn, retreating into video games. A regular client offers Kaitlyn a tempting job, but it would mean relocating to London. For Christmas she takes Adam back to Brian's family in the Colorado town of Hollowford to prepare their beloved, long-empty house for sale, wishing she could have five more minutes with her husband. At a local Christmas fair she meets Matthew (Bryant), a handsome former schoolmate and friend of Brian's, and they hit it off, but their budding relationship suffers when she learns he failed to disclose that he represents a large company that wants her house and land. His apology and his warm bond with Adam restore her trust, and he helps her fix up the house. Meanwhile, Adam has brief encounters every few days with a series of progressively older boys who mysteriously vanish, but not before drawing him into friendships, charity work and community life. When Kaitlyn agrees to sell and move to London, Adam, who wants to stay, pulls away, and in the basement she realises that the boys were Brian's spirit returning to help their son, before Brian appears and they share five minutes together.

The film was generally well received. TheWrap ranked it 14th of Hallmark's 43 new Christmas films of 2022, crediting Williams with injecting wit and life into a story that could have been a sappy bummer and praising her palpable chemistry with Bryant. Rebekah's Readings and Watchings gave it 8 out of 10, praising Williams's toned-down turn and the child actor. Cassandra Morgan found it more realistic and emotional than its predecessor, though she felt Adam was a little too good and the story too divided between mother and son.

Jaylen's life has changed dramatically since she won a singing competition and became one of the hottest new pop stars in the country. The attention has also brought her a stalker, and her record label hires Matt, a former Navy SEAL, to protect her. When she returns home for the holidays to her large, multi-generational family, the Rodriguezes, Jaylen knows that her loving but overprotective relatives, who already consider Los Angeles an unsafe place, would be alarmed to learn that she needs a security guard. She therefore introduces Matt as her new boyfriend and insists that he keep up the charade throughout the visit. The deception proves awkward for both of them: in addition to spending time with friends and family, Jaylen has a series of publicity events to attend, which makes Matt's job harder, and the serious, overzealous bodyguard struggles to relax as she wants him to while pretending to be in love. Staying with her family, Matt, a man used to a solitary life, gets to experience a Christmas full of warmth and family traditions, and comes to appreciate the support Jaylen enjoys. In turn, he helps her see that she should take control of her career rather than let her label dictate her music, as she wants to release songs in both English and Spanish despite the company's resistance. As the fake relationship continues, the two must decide whether to keep things strictly professional or admit to feelings that have become real.

The film premiered on Hallmark Channel on 4 December 2022. Reviews were lukewarm. Alonso Duralde of TheWrap, ranking all 43 of Hallmark's new Christmas films of 2022, placed it 32nd, describing it as a Hallmark fake-boyfriend movie crossed with The Bodyguard whose results were middling. Kristen of TV Tweetie enjoyed Jaylen as a strong, independent heroine who stands up to her family and label, and liked the depiction of the Rodriguez family's Christmas traditions, but found the film slow and unoriginal and did not recommend it.

Madison Rush (DeVitto), an actress eager to reinvent herself and move into directing, especially in the theatre, has co-written a play for a town's annual Christmas Eve production: a mock courtroom trial to decide the true authorship of the famous poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas", better known as "'Twas the Night Before Christmas", which is traditionally credited to Clement Clarke Moore (Austin-Olsen) but also claimed for Major Henry Livingston Jr. (Waugh). To draw audiences she recruits her friend and former co-star Connor Avery (Holtz), a charming actor who trained as a lawyer, acts to pay the bills and is a devoted father to his daughter, and who soon talks his way into the bed and breakfast where she is staying. Madison insists she does not date actors, but Connor keeps hinting that she was his favourite on-screen kiss. As the producer keeps throwing her curveballs, her co-writer has to leave for Los Angeles and the ghosts of Livingston and Moore turn up to argue their cases, Madison, who believes returning to the stage is what her late father would have wanted, struggles to hold the show together. When the troublesome lead actress, Lena (Bastelle), drops out the night before the performance, Connor and her friends help Madison see that she should play the lead herself, realising that she does not have to choose between acting and directing, and that she can date an actor after all.

TheWrap ranked it 10th of Hallmark's 43 new Christmas films of 2022, saying that although it tried to embrace many ideas, it somehow came together thanks mainly to the chemistry between DeVitto and Holtz. Erin E. Gross of Fangirlish also praised the leads' great on-screen chemistry and Madison's growth. Cassandra Morgan found it neither terrible nor good, arguing that it failed to make viewers care about the couple, the lead actress or the authorship mystery, which ended without a real resolution.

As children, Talia and Anderson were best friends who loved the classic Wunderbrook Christmas Story, a fairytale book given to Talia by her father shortly before he died. After his death Talia and her mother moved away, and although the two friends kept in touch for a time, thirty years pass without contact. Talia now runs a bookstore and has given up on her dream of becoming an author after repeated rejections from publishers, while Anderson is a surgeon shaken by the loss of his first patient as an attending physician. A chance meeting in her bookstore reunites them, and soon circumstances beyond their control bring both of them, along with other wayward guests, to the Gingerbread Inn in the cosy town of Wunderbrook, which looks curiously like the one in their beloved book. The guests include a married couple, Diane and Keith, who have lost their way, and Charles, an elderly widower afraid both of moving on and of being alone. The town's residents, led by Mayor Miles, have until Christmas Eve to set each visitor back on the right path during Wonder Week, a festival of tree lightings, markets and a mysterious procession, while the sharp-tongued Mildred plays her own part. As Talia sets out to solve the mystery of the town, she and Anderson rediscover their friendship and the possibility of something more.

The film premiered on Hallmark Channel on 3 December 2022. Brett White of Decider recommended it, likening the eerie town and its residents to Stephen King or the Endless of The Sandman and praising Prowse and Allan, while noting that Anderson never sparked as Talia did. Erin E. Gross of Fangirlish thought highly of it and hoped for sequels exploring Wunderbrook's secrets. Alonso Duralde of TheWrap ranked it 29th of Hallmark's 43 new holiday films, calling it a big swing but finding the leads miscast.

Molly (Grobglas) hopes to take over Gilbert's, her family's struggling, staunchly traditional deli on New York's Lower East Side, from her parents, if it does not go out of business first. Jacob (Jordan) is the heir to Zimmer's, a Los Angeles deli that has thrived by embracing modernity, serving fajitas and decorating with light-up menorahs, and his parents send him to New York to scout locations for a new franchise. The building he settles on turns out to be just down the street from Gilbert's. Meanwhile the two singletons' meddling grandmothers have signed them up with an elite Jewish matchmaker whose supposedly foolproof method requires clients to write longhand letters to an anonymous match. As Molly and Jacob spar in person over their rival businesses, they are also falling in love through their letters. Bonding over the scarcity of good Hanukkah songs and their families' stories of immigrant ancestors pursuing the American dream, the pair must discover whether their romance can survive their families' competing business interests, in a story that takes in a latke competition and climaxes with an old immigration tale.

The film was well received. TheWrap ranked it fourth of Hallmark's 43 new holiday films of 2022, describing it as a big bowl of The Shop Around the Corner with a dollop of Crossing Delancey and praising the lovely lead performances, Wolfe's sprightly screenplay and Loeb's new song. Talia Lakritz of Business Insider called it an authentic, delightful rom-com that finally got Hallmark's Hanukkah films right after earlier efforts that felt like Christmas movies with Jewish characters added as an afterthought. Irene Katz Connelly of the Forward found it schlocky but an indisputable improvement, with jokes that felt written by and for Jews, though she considered it essentially a knockoff of Nora Ephron's You've Got Mail.

Emily is a freelance copy editor who grew up on Evergreen Lane, a relentlessly festive street whose homeowners' association her parents shaped for decades with strict holiday rules, making her childhood Christmases feel like all work and no play. When her boyfriend breaks up with her, ruining her holiday plans, she accepts her parents' invitation to come home, only to learn on arrival that they are leaving for Florida, where they are house-hunting, and that she will spend Christmas alone in her childhood home. Without the decorations her parents normally put up, the house falls foul of the HOA, now led by Jared, an architect and Emily's childhood friend, who keeps arriving at her door with citations and a tape measure. Pressed by Jared and a collection of quirky neighbours, including Ned, who initiates her into "Team Kringle", and the exacting Pamela, Emily is drawn into the neighbourhood's many traditions: a Christmas carnival, a tree lighting, a snowman tableau and a cookie contest. As she decorates the house and takes part, she finds Jared's childlike Christmas devotion oddly charming, comes to understand why her parents valued service to the community during the holidays, and grows closer to him.

The film premiered on Hallmark Channel in November 2022. Brett White of Decider called it a quick-witted treat that succeeded by committing fully to the classic Hallmark format, praising Tobolowsky and Peterman as possibly the two funniest performances of the season and declaring Chabert the network's holiday queen. Alonso Duralde of TheWrap ranked it third of Hallmark's 43 new holiday films of 2022 for its genuine laughs, while Jodi Walker of The Ringer enjoyed the supporting cast but found the neighbourhood's pressure on Emily cult-like, comparing it to Midsommar.

Ella Chapel (Greenwood), a graphic designer who moved from Pennsylvania to Boston two years earlier, returns home to Mary's Town for the holidays to a family still struggling after the death of her grandfather Riley (Gray), who served as the town's mayor, championed its annual Kwanzaa celebrations and long acted as the family peacemaker. Her visit begins with a shock when her mother Micah (Robinson Peete) announces that she is moving to Chicago after the holidays to open her own bistro. Micah and her mother Tess (Cooke) run the Chapel Family Bakery together but are barely speaking: Tess, uninterested in celebrating this year, throws herself into work around the clock and clings to her traditional recipes, refusing to give Micah any say in the business, even though Micah has worked there since high school. Determined to heal the rift and keep her mother in town, Ella digs out her grandfather's Kwanzaa chest and sets out to get the whole family to observe all seven nights of the holiday alongside their Christmas traditions. She is helped by her ex-boyfriend Griffin (Darnell), now the mayor, who is carrying on the town's Kwanzaa events, and as the pair scheme to get Micah and Tess talking, they also confront why Ella left and what their relationship might become.

Reviews were mixed. Decider recommended it as a heartwarming film, praising the extraordinary chemistry of Greenwood, Robinson Peete and Cooke as three generations of Chapel women, the focus on family rather than romance, Plowman's propulsive score and the respectful depiction of Kwanzaa. TheWrap ranked it 23rd of Hallmark's 43 new holiday films of 2022, calling it a step in the right direction that explained the holiday gracefully, though neither the family drama nor the love story leapt off the page. Kristen of TV Tweetie liked its celebration of Kwanzaa but found the scenes between Tess and Micah hard to watch and the film boring.

The special retells the familiar story through the eyes of Belle, a kind, book-loving young woman who is imprisoned by the Beast, a prince transformed by an enchantress as punishment for his arrogance. In the enchanted castle she befriends its servants, who have been turned into household objects, and gradually comes to care for her captor, while the vain hunter Gaston schemes to win her as his wife. Scenes from the animated film are interwoven with newly staged versions of its songs, reinterpreted by the cast and more than thirty dancers in styles ranging from breakdance and ballet to contemporary and ballroom, along with numbers not featured in the animated version. Paige O'Hara and Richard White, the original voices of Belle and Gaston, and composer Alan Menken appear in cameos during "Belle". Twain sang the title song with Menken at the piano as a tribute to Angela Lansbury, the original Mrs. Potts, who had died weeks earlier, and H.E.R. closed the show performing it on electric guitar.

Announced in July 2022, the special was filmed on the Disney lot in Burbank in November 2022, with choreography by Jamal Sims and Derek Hough, production design by Julio Himede, who adapted sketches from the studio's archives as projected backdrops, and more than 400 costumes by Marina Toybina. H.E.R., the first African-Filipino woman to play a Disney princess on screen, also served as a producer and worked with Menken on the arrangements. It aired on 15 December 2022 and streamed the next day on Disney+ and Hulu, drawing 4.26 million viewers. Reviews were generally positive: Esquire and TVLine praised H.E.R. and the surprising Twain, and Entertainment Weekly ranked it third among all live television musicals, calling the sets and costumes magical.

Gail Travers (Cepero), a singer who performs mostly cover songs, has spent a year living in an old Volkswagen bus she has named Jewel, travelling the country to play small gigs and open mic nights while dreaming of stardom. Encouraged by a friend, she submits a performance video to a contest and wins the chance to perform at iHeartRadio's Christmas Eve concert in Los Angeles, but she must drive across the country in two weeks and write an original song along the way, scraping together poorly paid gigs and documenting the trip for her social media followers. In Oklahoma she swerves to avoid an alpaca in the road and crashes her van, stranding her in the small town of Harmony Springs. The alpaca belongs to Van (Shields), who owns the local auto-repair shop, and her son Jeremy (Sumpter), a handsome mechanic and local jack-of-all-trades. Unable to afford the repairs, Gail follows Jeremy's advice, picking up karaoke work and becoming the music teacher for a group of misfit children at the local school who hope to perform in a Christmas Eve gala of their own. As she works on her new song, contends with Jeremy's jealous ex-girlfriend and grows close to him and the town, Gail realises that fulfilling her lifelong dream may mean leaving behind the man and the community she has come to love.

Reviews were negative. John Serba of Decider recommended skipping it, calling it dull, wholesome background viewing with a contrived plot built on coincidences and 25 more minutes than usual in which nothing dramatically compelling happens, though he felt Cepero, who sings well, showed promise and deserved a better script. Nicole Ackman of Ready Steady Cut rated it 2.5 out of 5, describing an average low-budget Christmas film elevated only by Cepero's lovely voice and its original Christmas song, while criticising the weaker acting of Shields and Sumpter, the predictable story, the slow first half and its conspicuous iHeartRadio product placement.

Jessica is a young, up-and-coming Hollywood filmmaker who has made a name for herself directing Christmas movies, a genre she has loved since childhood. While she is shooting her seventh holiday romance, a formulaic tale about a small-town bakery owner facing eviction by a heartless big-city developer, filmed in the heat of a Los Angeles July, the handsome numbers man Christopher arrives on set. He announces that, in a shake-up at the network, the Christmas movie division is closing in favour of thrillers, which means her current production will be her last for the company, and that he will stay to oversee and cut her budget. Jessica instantly despises him, but Reena points out the irony: Jessica is not only trying to save her Christmas movie, she is living in one, with all its classic tropes. To get both her film and her life to their happy endings, Jessica must juggle her not very bright leading actors as they fall in and out of love, a wayward elf dog, a mediocre script she must fix without breaking the formula, a shortage of money and her own stirring feelings for her perceived nemesis, while learning to let go of her perfectionism, even as she discovers that the network is taking desperate measures to shut her down.

The film was released on HBO Max on 1 December 2022. Brett White of Decider gave it a timid "skip it", enjoying its sharp early jokes about how such films are made, the chemistry between Van and Swickard and the comic performances of Borrego and Dandy, but finding that it lost energy as the romance took over. Rahul Shinde of The Envoy considered it self-aware but rushed, with underdeveloped character arcs, and Barbara Shulgasser-Parker of Common Sense Media found it a tad cleverer than most holiday fluff and mindlessly enjoyable in a mundane way.

Tracey Wise (Lilley) is a renowned luxury travel blogger with a large following, whose cheerful motto is that people can travel more if they travel wisely. One of her fans is Graham Cooper (Hutch), who helps his mother Barbara (Williams) run Silver Peak, a small family bed and breakfast in Vermont. Since a big upscale hotel resort opened nearby and began stealing their guests, the business has been struggling to survive, so Graham invites Tracey and her boyfriend Mark (Preston) on a Christmas getaway at the inn in exchange for a review. Just before the trip, Tracey learns of a potential job at a renowned travel magazine that requires a sample review, and since she is already heading to Vermont she decides to review the rival luxury hotel as well, planning to stay there first. When Graham bumps into her at a local coffee shop, however, he assumes she has arrived early and drives her straight to the B&B before she can explain, and she cannot bring herself to admit that she and Mark have just broken up, turning the romantic getaway into a trip for one. As the only guest, Tracey is lavished with attention by Barbara and her sister Sarah (Twa), who go overboard trying to make everything perfect and, once the truth about Mark comes out, notice a spark between Tracey and Graham and give the pair space. As Tracey falls for both the inn and Graham, her secret review of the competing hotel threatens to cause conflict.

Reviews were mixed. Kristen of TV Tweetie judged it "quietly good", a charming, relaxing film with a small cast and a narrow focus on romance, and found both leads natural, with perfect chemistry. Sneha Jaiswal of Abstract AF rated it 2 out of 5, praising its beautiful, festive Christmas settings and the fun older actors playing the matchmaking sisters, but finding the plot predictable within fifteen minutes, Lilley's portrayal lacking warmth and the leads devoid of chemistry, despite Hutch making a worthy romantic hero.

Abigale is a dating coach and aspiring self-help author who is on the verge of publishing her first book, a how-to guide to dating over the holidays. When she meets the publisher Jack, however, he argues that people should not need a guide to find love, because fate will bring the right two people together on their own. Abigale counters that times have changed and that there are tips worth following, and to prove that her advice really works she makes a bet with him: she will make a man fall for her within twelve days and bring him to Jack's Christmas Eve party as proof, in return for a book deal. She sets out following her own rules, which include not seeing a date two days in a row, staying mysterious and getting to know someone only lightly, but with so little time she is soon forced to bend them. When she meets Michael Ryan at a bar, she breaks one immediately by agreeing to a date straight away, and as their romance develops she sees him too often, learns too much about him, meets his friends too soon and falls too fast, although he falls just as quickly. Along the way she realises that sometimes it is better to follow one's instincts and be spontaneous, and that there is something underhanded about making someone fall in love as a test to advance her career. When Michael learns of the bet at the worst possible moment, he feels used, and Abigale must try to make things right before Christmas.
