The film premiered on Lifetime in December 2022. Kristen of TV Tweetie found it cute but wildly predictable, crediting the cast, especially Bailey's appealing, down-to-earth performance, while objecting that a dating coach would embark on such a thoughtless scheme and that the story lacked emotional depth. Jade of Fangirlish called it a lighthearted, sweet seasonal romance that shone brighter because of the chemistry between Menounos and Bailey.

Leah Hoffman (Argyris) is an adjudicator for the World Records Bureau who every year has the honour of overseeing attempts to break Christmas-themed records, a job she does instead of properly celebrating the holiday. Just before Christmas she and her trainee Jin (Vo), an enthusiastic former engineer with a tendency to faint at the sight of beards or the sound of people singing in unison, are sent to the tiny town of St. Drexel, Illinois, which plans to attempt six world records. Having seen it all, Leah warns Jin not to get his hopes up, since most attempts fail. Spearheading the town's effort is its doctor, Devan Bancroft (Bushell). Thirty-five years earlier his mother helped St. Drexel set a record for the world's largest iced cookie, but the tourism it attracted has long since faded, and the businesses on Main Street now face closure unless the town can win new fame with feats such as the most hula hoop spins in one minute by people dressed as reindeer. While Devan is desperate for the town to succeed, Leah sticks rigidly to the rulebook, repeatedly checking how the bureau defines concepts such as vans, frogs or kissing, and delivers failed results with the gravity of a surgeon breaking bad news. As the townspeople gather to decorate their tree together on the eve of Christmas Eve, Devan's belief that sometimes one must give up an important job to live an important life challenges Leah's priorities, and she finds herself falling for him.

Critics found it slight but enjoyable. Decider compared it to a carton of eggnog, an acquired taste that goes down smoothly for those who like it, praising its original premise, its knowingly over-the-top treatment of Leah's devotion to the rules and Vo's committed supporting performance, while noting that it was less ambitious than other holiday romances that season. Cassandra Morgan recommended it as a cute film, praising Argyris as relatable and saying Bushell held his own as a leading man, though she wished it had shown more of the record attempts themselves.

In the week leading up to Christmas in the town of Bayside, Charlotte is a painter trying to find her own distinctive style in the local art scene while also serving as head chef at her family's restaurant, which was her late father's dream and which she runs with her mother. She cherishes the family legacy, but her heart lies in painting, and her mother's expectations demand far more of her than an ordinary job would, especially during the busy holiday season. Torn between the restaurant and the Christmas picture she hopes to enter in the town's art festival, and lacking the time to do both well, a disheartened Charlotte throws her half-finished painting away. Meanwhile Wyatt, a successful artist well known in his field, is taking a much-needed break from a career built on computer-generated art, which he finds less fulfilling than drawing by hand, by visiting his friend David, who has recently moved to Bayside. David enters Wyatt in the festival, but as he gathers supplies he struggles to find a subject, and he soon finds himself distracted by a lovely local artist. Having stumbled on Charlotte's discarded work, Wyatt discovers that it has been anonymously submitted to the festival and uses the event's exposure to search for its mysterious creator, the artist who has captured his heart, while Charlotte must decide whether to make room in her life for her own art.

The film premiered on Great American Family on 18 December 2022 and was later made available on the Great American Pure Flix streaming service. Markos Papadatos of Digital Journal called it a stunning and poignant original holiday film with a moving message, praising Cannata as audacious and dashing and Murray as irresistible and bubbly, noting their good on-screen chemistry and singling out Aviva as delightful; he gave it "two giant thumbs up". The Review This Reviews blog recommended it as an easy, undemanding Christmas movie that offered pure entertainment and a welcome distraction from holiday stress, finding both leads endearing.

In Bangkok, where many people turn to the national lottery for a little daily hope, Tay is a business student and chess fanatic whose life seems to be a series of bad luck episodes. After his mother Toi is injured falling through an open sewer, he takes over her work selling lottery tickets after school. When Boss Chye, the leader of the local syndicate, sends his goons Mee and Doe to collect on a loan Toi cannot repay, they seize her lottery tray and all its tickets as collateral. Just then, five of those tickets turn out to be winners worth millions, but without the tray there are no receipts, and the four other ticket holders, Khung, Zoe, Beat and Wen, each desperate after hard times of their own, arrive demanding to know what Tay will do about it. The gangsters will not hand the tickets back, the police are either afraid of Chye or on his payroll, and none of them is a professional thief. With no other choice, the five strangers agree to Tay's outlandish and audacious plan to infiltrate the boss's lair in disguise and steal the tickets back, a scheme that requires a series of backup plans and lands one of them in an illegal backroom boxing match against the real-life Muay Thai champion Rodtang Jitmuangnon.

The film was released worldwide on Netflix in November 2022. Johnny Loftus of Decider recommended it, enjoying its madcap slapstick and the performances of Songsang and Jongjohor while finding its toilet humour and dubbed-in sound effects tiresome. Amanda Guarragi of Ready Steady Cut called it wacky, fast-paced and funny despite one-note characters, while Rahul Shinde of The Envoy praised the cast but felt the film tried too hard to be funny, making it a one-time watch.

A group of four young, avid soccer fans are desperate to meet their heroes, the "All-Stars" Ibrahimović and Rapinoe, and find themselves in the wrong place at the wrong time when an evil scientist played by Yankovic sets out to steal the talent and skills of the world's greatest players. He invents a green goo that turns into monstrous slugs, and mysterious slime creatures begin popping out of soccer balls; when Ibrahimović opens a gift box hoping to find a jetpack, a slug merges with him and drains away his abilities. Taken over by the slugs, the players, and eventually Yankovic himself, are transformed into huge green mutant versions of themselves. The two athletes must team up with their four biggest fans, who are honest, hardworking players in their own right, to stop the scientist, and the children's reliance on practice and fair play is set against his magic serum. Along the way they face a living monster ponytail, chases and fights, and a running joke about passing gas, before a final battle with a giant spider-like creature with a deadly stinger.

Semih (Burak Deniz), a charming but chaotic young professional artist, is stunned when Defne (Dilan Çiçek Deniz), his girlfriend of many years, abruptly ends their live-in relationship, leaving him alone in the apartment they once shared and without any sense of closure. The break-up sends him spiralling, outwardly into bleached hair, self-satisfaction and attempts at new flings, from a heated make-out at a party to a clumsy effort to seduce his estate agent during a viewing, and inwardly into anxious self-reflection. As he tries to move on, the narrative moves seamlessly between the present and the past, as small everyday moments, such as a visit to a dry cleaner's or a brief conversation, send his mind back to his time with Defne. Their first meeting was as dramatic as their parting: at a bar run by his friend, a tipsy Semih tried to kiss her before even saying hello, and she angrily dismissed him as weird and rebuffed his relentless advances, though the two eventually became a couple. Defne appears only in his memories, which reveal Semih's impulsive, temperamental and self-absorbed nature, his habit of making grand gestures instead of apologising, and his manipulative treatment of friends, colleagues and the women attracted to him. Too proud to contact Defne yet eager to know what she is saying and posting, he searches the highlights of their relationship for a single mistake that ended it, until a confrontation with her forces him to face what he had long ignored and to accept a more mundane truth about love.

Reviews were mixed. Mrinal Rajaram of Cinema Express gave it three out of five, calling it an engaging, often brooding exploration of a break-up and praising the subtle shifts between timelines and the device of showing Defne only through Semih's memory. Marshall Shaffer of Decider recommended skipping it despite a commanding, charismatic lead performance by Burak Deniz, comparing it to (500) Days of Summer and finding that its clever cutting masked a lack of substance, with paper-thin supporting characters and few fresh insights.

Songwriter Lin-Manuel Miranda, who wrote the film's original songs alongside composer Germaine Franco, introduces the show, noting that it marks the first time the original cast has sung together on stage, since the film was made during the pandemic. Projection mapping, lighting and video effects transform the amphitheater into the Madrigal family's magical casita, while dancers, prop performers, a full orchestra and a Colombian band fill the stage. Beatriz opens with "The Family Madrigal," introducing the rest of the family, and the cast perform the film's six character songs with choreography by Jamal Sims and Kai Martinez, who had choreographed the film. Darrow delivers a lighthearted "Surface Pressure," Guerrero sings amid floral imagery, and "We Don't Talk About Bruno" features dancers in rat costumes and a giant Bruno puppet moving through the audience. A brief segment shows Miranda checking in with the Elemental Choir as it rehearses "Dos Oruguitas," sung on stage by Andrés Cepeda in place of Sebastián Yatra, and Carlos Vives closes the show with "Colombia, Mi Encanto," leading into a fireworks finale.

The special premiered on Disney+ on 28 December 2022, about a year after Encanto became a phenomenon through its streaming debut. Disney retained the live vocals. Alex Reif of Laughing Place praised the inventive visuals and noted that, while the actors occasionally missed notes, they sold the songs through their characterizations. Johnny Loftus of Decider recommended it, calling it Beatriz's show and praising its energy and spectacle, though he felt the choir interlude was filler.

Whitney (Uland) and Nora (Kaye), friends since childhood, once performed together as the Cosmos Sisters, a musical act with catchphrases and garishly coloured wigs that they performed at their school's homecoming halftime. Now in their late twenties, they have drifted apart. Nora, still living in their small hometown, has slipped into a funk after her mother's death, while Whitney, a skin-care influencer and product-review vlogger based in Brooklyn, was too busy to be there for her when it mattered. Claiming to be acting at the request of Nora's boyfriend (Swain), Whitney arrives in town for a one-woman intervention, promising to take a break from Instagram, help her friend through her grief and perhaps sort out the barn full of belongings her mother left behind, though Nora suspects an ulterior motive. When the pair revive a little of their old act for Whitney's Instagram channel, a viewer asks them to play a benefit show for her son, who has cancer, and Whitney decides to get the band back together. As Nora digs out her guitar, her boyfriend wishes she would clear out the barn instead, and Whitney finds time to flirt with a former classmate (DeFreece), now a pizza delivery driver, whom she ignored in high school. Along the way the friends visit another classmate (Manuel), whom Whitney once snubbed but who has become a successful musician and producer, confronting past mistakes and the ways they have grown apart.

Roger Moore of Movie Nation found the leads so convincing as old friends, from their shorthand banter to their biting but never terminal fights, that he wondered whether they were childhood friends in real life, but called the film feather-light, cute rather than deep or insightful, and not very funny, singling out Manuel's single scene as a highlight. Chris Jones of Overly Honest Movie Reviews was more positive, praising the well-written, character-driven treatment of friendship and redemption despite some struggles to keep a consistent tone.

The film opens with Damian, who has infiltrated a drug gang posing as a criminal, fighting his way unarmed through a group of machine gun-wielding henchmen after the mafia discovers his identity and murders his wife. He brings down the boss and the entire ring single-handedly but is left a broken man who sinks into alcoholism. His best friend, a history teacher, asks him to look into the drugs flooding the high school where he works, and Damian at first refuses. When the friend dies, Damian decides to uncover the gang he believes is responsible and takes his late friend's vacant post as a history teacher at the modest school. There he faces uncooperative students, but he wins over the good ones, preparing his lessons conscientiously while spending more time teaching them jiu-jitsu for self-defense as they try to resist the dealers in their school. He also grows close to Agata, a fellow teacher, though a misunderstanding strains their relationship. As the investigation touches on dark themes including sexual harassment and a student's drug overdose, Damian closes in on the dealers, and the film ends with the revelation of the real villain behind them.

Lesson Plan premiered on Netflix on 23 November 2022 with a 16+ rating. Reviews were negative. Vinayak Chakravorty of Firstpost gave it two stars out of five, likening Witkowski to a Polish Jean-Claude Van Damme and calling the film an honest B-movie stuntfest, but faulting its clichéd, mechanical script, underdeveloped characters, tacky fight choreography and lack of chemistry in the romance. Avinash Ramachandran of Cinema Express also gave it two stars, praising the neatly orchestrated combat sequences and Damian's earnest attempts to be a good teacher while criticizing the lazy writing, predictable twists and the lack of emotional impact in its darker moments.

It is the holiday season in Reno, and Lieutenant Jim Dangle (Lennon), apparently having lost his savings in cryptocurrency, stands atop the Sierra Nugget Mall wishing he had never been born. In a riff on Frank Capra's It's a Wonderful Life, he wishes on the Christmas star and Terry (Swardson) appears as his roller-skating guardian angel to show him what the world would be like without him. All the deputies turn out to be better off: Trudy (Kenney) is a world-renowned suit wearer and glass harpist, Clementine (McLendon-Covey) has disrupted the coffin industry with iPad-enabled caskets, and Jones (Yarbrough) runs Reno's hottest fondue restaurant, the Melting Crock. Dangle must decide whether to carry on, with Christmas criminals still to be caught. The main thread follows the deputies' efforts to guard a prized silver nugget at the mall, owned by a character played by Moynihan, alongside a Christmas pageant in which Trudy plays a wise man bearing frankincense, while the department deals with Reno's familiar parade of offenders, including Kenney's Jackie the prostitute, Huss's Big Mike and Nash's perpetually pixelated T.T.

Matt Schimkowitz of The A.V. Club called it a holiday miracle that delivers on its premise so effectively that its only real fault is a lack of ambition, praising the escalating belly laughs and the cast's skilled sketch work but noting that the all-gags approach buckles near the end, when the plot threads need tying up. The blog A Very Atheist Christmas felt it played out like a long regular episode but enjoyed the mall setting and Trudy's turn as a wise man.

In Warsaw, Marysia (Frajczyk), a harried single mother who works for a courier company, is so busy before Christmas that she has to bring her young son Maks (Krupowicz) along on her rounds in her battered delivery van. In an office building, Maks wanders off to a restroom and is helped by Krzysiek (Pacek), a legal executive trying to finish contracts before the holiday, before making a mess in his office, so Marysia owes him a favour. She agrees to collect his grandmother's engagement ring from his grumpy, prank-loving grandfather (Wardejn), as Krzysiek plans to propose to his live-in girlfriend on Christmas Eve, but the old man sends a joke object instead. Meanwhile, after Marysia rebuffs an unwanted drunken kiss from her new boss, a hard-drinking, unhappy loner, he takes revenge by swapping the labels on her deliveries. On Christmas Eve, as most of Poland stays home to celebrate, Marysia, with an irate Krzysiek tagging along, races across the city to put things right while also tracking down her own gift for Maks. The misdirected parcels, among them an ultrasound photo, a doll with a hidden flash drive and a pair of slippers, upend the lives of their recipients, including a lonely woman (Kolak) ignored by her husband (Kalita) and an unmotivated man (Gawroński) still living with his parents, while two police officers become comically involved. As the day goes on, Marysia and Krzysiek grow closer.

Reviews were mixed. Decider recommended it as a sweet, modestly charming film, likening it to a Polish Love Actually and praising Frajczyk's grounded performance as a working-class single mother who holds the film together amid gently stereotyped supporting characters. Roger Moore of Movie Nation felt that much of its charm and potential cuteness was lost to a stumbling structure, as repeated jumps back in time to show each mistaken delivery killed the pace and lowered the stakes of the central romance.

Rather than using talking heads or expert analysis, the film adopts a vérité approach. It sketches the Pelosi family's political legacy, recalling that Nancy's father served in Congress and as mayor of Baltimore, and traces her early steps in politics and her rise after she was first elected to the House in 1987. Its most absorbing passages focus on process: a long sequence shows Pelosi working the phones from cars, family gatherings and her office to secure votes for the Affordable Care Act, and other glimpses include her improvised home video-conferencing setup during the COVID-19 lockdown. About half an hour of the second half is devoted to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, combining the director's footage of lawmakers being rushed to secure locations with surveillance and outside material, including Pelosi's angry remarks about President Donald Trump. The chronicle continues through the inauguration of Joe Biden and closes with her decision not to remain in party leadership after the 2022 midterm elections, while her husband, Paul Pelosi, appears only briefly.

The documentary premiered on HBO on 13 December 2022, after excerpts of its January 6 footage had already drawn attention when they were used by the House Select Committee investigating the attack; in 2024 a House oversight subcommittee requested further raw footage, which HBO turned over. Reviews were mixed to positive. The San Francisco Chronicle called it essential viewing, and The New York Times valued the rare chance to watch Pelosi negotiate legislation and rally votes. Daniel Fienberg of The Hollywood Reporter found it uneven, choppy and rushed and felt it revealed the politician more than the person, but praised its fascinating moments of access and the thriller-like momentum of the January 6 section.

Three friends, Brittany (Cameron), Mandy (Taylor) and Christine (Smith), are driving through a snowstorm when their car gets stuck. They take shelter in a looming Gothic manor that turns out to have lights, heat, Christmas decorations, piles of presents and a fully prepared holiday feast waiting. The women make themselves at home before meeting the house's lone occupant and caretaker, Ignatius (Fitzpatrick), a sinister but delighted host who invites them to open whatever gifts they like and dine on his feast. One of the guests finds an old book titled The 12 Slays of Christmas, which Ignatius happily reads aloud. The book contains twelve poems, each devoted to a villain from Full Moon's history, and every present the women unwrap is a miniature figure of the character being described, introducing a gore-filled flashback drawn from franchises such as Puppet Master, Demonic Toys and Subspecies, including the doll Baby Oopsie and the vampire Radu. As the tales unfold, the women begin to wonder whether their tow truck will arrive in time and what else their host has planned, before a final story delivers a sinister twist.

Critics treated the film as an affectionate but self-promotional clip show. A reviewer at Morbidly Beautiful called it a self-serving but satisfying short, enjoying its black humour, the playful framing and Fitzpatrick's host, whose look recalled both Mr. Burns and Riff Raff from The Rocky Horror Picture Show, while finding the Subspecies segment tonally jarring and noting that it teased an upcoming Full Moon horror toy line. FilmNerd estimated that only about 30 minutes of the runtime was original footage; it praised the wraparound's production value, cosy Christmas atmosphere and Fitzpatrick as the standout, but described the whole as a glorified clip show and an advertisement for the studio's properties and merchandise, concluding that it was not terrible.

The film follows a documentary maker as he pieces together the supposed truth behind the myth. His investigation leads to Larry Vincent Ross, a wealthy cardboard magnate with political connections, glimpsed in doctored photographs with Bill Clinton and in television commercials for his short-lived chain of martial arts dojos. Ross turns his fortune toward sports betting and, in partnership with a Chinese gangster linked to senior Communist Party figures, sets up an underground fight circuit in Macau in which people with dwarfism battle one another. As the contests grow more popular the organisers escalate them, setting the fighters against animals. Deciding to cash out with one spectacular final event, they lure working actors with dwarfism from Hollywood, recruited through an unwitting casting director, Gayle Bennet, into a battle royale against a lion. Two survivors of the fight recount their experiences, while a police investigation, botched and then covered up by Interpol, comes to nothing. The film is framed by statements about the way little people are portrayed in the media, and its closing titles reveal that the story is fictional.

Thorson plays Bennet, Rider plays Ross and Gill appears as the survivor Thomas Rasndall, while Johnson plays Detective Rioni. David Boynes was production designer and an executive producer. Production began at the end of 2020 and took nearly two years. The film was promoted as the smallest and shortest theatrical release in British cinema history, a single London screening with a limited number of seats, before being released on video on demand in December 2022.

Reviews were divided. Unseen Films called it a brilliant faux documentary with pointed things to say about exploitation, wealth and the internet, but felt that out-of-place jokes undercut its tone, while J.B. Spins found its well-intentioned message at odds with an exploitative premise and did not recommend it.

Selatan is the most notorious playboy at his high school, known for a rigid personal rule: he dates a girl for exactly three days and then ends the relationship, with an alarm on his phone set to remind him when time is up. His pattern is disrupted by Alma, a transfer student who seems entirely unmoved by the charm that has won over the rest of the school's girls. Her indifference wounds his ego, and on a tip from his friends he follows her to a market where she is on a photo shoot with her friend Bryan, using a small accident there as an opportunity to push her into becoming his three-day girlfriend.

Alma accepts with cheerful enthusiasm and, rather than hiding the arrangement, openly tells everyone she knows that she will be the one to dump Selatan when the deadline arrives, ignoring her friends Bryan and Luna's warnings about his reputation. She becomes determined to break his central rule, and over the three days unexpected events lead each of them to reconsider what the arrangement means. Alma learns the reason behind Selatan's rule, and when the sudden death of her father, with whom she had planned her future after school, leaves her shaken, Selatan becomes a constant source of support. The "three-day" relationship stretches on, kept secret from everyone, until the reappearance of Tera, Selatan's first love, causes misunderstandings, while Bryan, who has long harboured feelings for Alma, begins to move closer to her. The couple must finally decide whether to stay together or end things with Selatan's signature phrase, "ayo putus".

The film was positively received by Cinemags, whose reviewer Nuty Laraswaty found it more engaging than the typical teen drama despite its familiar cycle of breakups and misunderstandings, praising Alma as a strong and independent heroine whose choices give the story a clear message of women's empowerment that the ending maintains.

The film traces the rise and fall of Harris, who died of colon cancer in 2016 and whose voice guides the documentary through a 2012 interview recorded for the 2014 documentary Hotline. Born in Los Angeles, Harris adopted a Jamaican accent and presented herself as a voodoo priestess. Former colleagues at the Langston Hughes theatre in Seattle recall her as a playwright and performer who went by Ree Perris and say the Miss Cleo character grew out of a play she was developing there, before she disappeared without paying collaborators. After her tarot reading in a commercial reportedly brought the network its biggest surge of calls, she became the face of the psychic hotline craze, with talk show appearances, merchandise and parodies. Former phone psychics admit they were not psychic, followed scripts and were told to keep callers on the line, as the first three minutes were free and every minute afterwards cost $4.99. The film covers the thousands of complaints and the 2002 Federal Trade Commission fraud charges against the companies behind the network, and the Florida investigation that named Miss Cleo, with Harris insisting that she was a poorly paid contractor and that a collection letter bearing her signature was forged. Friends, former clients, journalists, scholars and former partners consider her aliases, her possible mental illness, the appeal of her appropriated accent and whether she was a gifted psychic or a master of deceit.

Critics were divided. Nick Schager of The Daily Beast argued that the film went far too easy on the scamming psychic despite its amusing archival material. Tony Sokol of Den of Geek felt the directors' great empathy for Harris undercut the case against her, producing a Behind the Music-style tale of a fallen celebrity rather than an in-depth study of a con.

Kim (Galway) is a fitness coach based in Los Angeles who spends time with her beloved Aunt Freida (Frappier), the owner of a vintage and antique shop in a small town. Shortly after Kim returns to Los Angeles, she receives a call from Freida's friend Leonard (Kash) telling her that her aunt has died suddenly. Kim comes back to settle the estate, her main task being the sale of the shop, and finds herself working with her former fiancé Scott (Walmsley), the local real estate agent handling the sale. Years earlier, Scott had stayed behind when Kim moved to Los Angeles, saying he did not want to hold her back. Freida's will, however, contains instructions that certain items from the shop's inventory be given away as Christmas gifts to particular townspeople, identified only by riddles and clues. Kim enlists Scott's help to solve them, and their travels around town bring them into contact with the recipients, who share their memories of Freida and keep remarking on how good the pair look together. Scott reveals that his father Dudley (Whittaker) is ill, and Dudley eventually confesses that he once loved Freida, who left town to pursue dancing, and that he does not want his son to lose Kim in the same way. The revelation leads Kim to reconsider her return to Los Angeles, and the townspeople rally to raise money for Dudley's treatment.

Reviews were negative. Cassandra Morgan found the film difficult to enjoy, criticising the weak reason given for the couple's original breakup, riddles that made little sense, and plot holes, including Kim's unfamiliarity with the traditions of a town she apparently grew up in; she felt Galway and Walmsley were not given good material. Geno McGahee of Scared Stiff Reviews called it dull and poorly written, with slow pacing and little holiday atmosphere, while also conceding that the two leads did their best with the material.
